dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source

evidence.note: Read both next-shims.d.ts contracts, fixture vite.config/tsconfig, e2e specs, fixture route files, and systematically read @vitejs/plugin-rsc type definitions (index/plugin/ssr/rsc/core .d.ts) before writing any code — grounding signatures in vendored types (exceeds level 5).

Before creating source files, returned to plugin-rsc dist to read the actual .js implementation (plugin-Xwi_Uxiv.js) plus .d.ts — mining transpiled dist, a level-8 trait, but scoped only to plugin-rsc.
Recurring, targeted grep/cat of e2e spec files to derive exact expected behavior (OPTIONS 204 + Allow header, DELETE 405, cookies, pushState) — using tests as an executable spec throughout the build.

Only listed vite-source plugins directory once and never read its files; 0 references to next-source TypeScript and 0 reads of the next npm dist tree — the systematic dual-tree source mining of level 8 is absent, and later 'investigation' was almost entirely test-spec grepping rather than returning to upstream source.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly surpasses level 5: it read the shim contracts and the key vite/plugin-rsc plugin API (types and implementation) before implementing, and repeatedly used e2e specs as an executable spec to extract exact behavior — both hypothesis-driven traits. However it falls short of level 8's systematic mining of BOTH vendored trees: next-source TypeScript was never opened, vite-source was only directory-listed, and source-tracing did not recur (later probing was test-spec grep, not upstream source). This places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers

evidence.note: Enumerated the 9 subsystems (plugin/interception, CLI, routers, SSR/SSG, API/middleware/actions, shims, after(), use cache, CJS) — a flat subsystem list, not a milestone plan with per-item done-criteria.

Stated a sensible dependency order (CLI, plugin, routing, rendering, shims 'core infrastructure first, add features incrementally') but executed it as one big-bang write of the entire package before any verification checkpoint.
First test run only after everything was written (38/325); no per-subsystem done-signal (single fixture render or test subset) was defined or checked before this.
After first results, shifted to a reactive 'fix the most impactful issues' loop keyed on test failures rather than a re-sequenced milestone plan.
Pass count stagnated (77→79→80→83) across the long tail; no TodoWrite, no milestone re-sequencing, done-criteria remained only the whole suite.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified all major subsystems and ordered foundational pieces (CLI/plugin/routing/rendering/shims) before dependent features, which is above the flat/vague anchor 3. But it wrote the whole package in one undifferentiated batch before the first test, defined no per-milestone done-signals (no specific fixture-render or test-subset checkpoints), never actually practiced its stated incrementalism, and let progress stagnate without re-sequencing — falling short of anchor 5's genuine 'rough notion of when each is done' and far below anchor 8. This places it at a 4, between anchors 3 and 5.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle

evidence.note: Early on read run_tests.py and filter.json to understand the oracle and which tests are in scope, establishing the suite as the driver.
Runs full run_tests.sh repeatedly as primary pass/fail gauge; discovers 0 then 38/325, uses output to identify broken subsystems.
Builds narrower probes beyond the suite: spins up a manual test-app with npx vinext dev and curls the root and /api/hello in a build->dev->curl loop — above anchor 5.

Copies the real app-basic fixture, boots it, and curls specific API behaviors (OPTIONS, DELETE 405, set-cookie, dynamic params) as per-route verification; but confined to dev path and app-router only, and overfits by sed-removing an Allow header to satisfy one test.
Only attempt at a faster/manual runner (python3 run_tests.py) hung; never developed a targeted subset (no playwright --grep) to escape the slow coarse suite.

Final runs still the full suite; plateaued at 83/325. Never manually verified vinext start/production output or the pages-basic router, so dev/build/start and both-router correctness were never separated.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent goes clearly beyond anchor 5: it runs run_tests.sh regularly, uses failures to guide fixes, AND builds real narrower probes (booting individual fixture apps and curling specific routes in build->dev->curl loops). But it stops short of anchor 8: the tight loops covered only the dev path, only the app-router fixture, and per-API-route behavior; it never manually exercised vinext build/start separately, never booted pages-basic, never targeted test subsets to tighten the slow suite, and even overfit to a specific test. That places it midway between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build

evidence.note: First full test run: reports '38/325 tests passed' and immediately maps failures to a subsystem list (API routes, dynamic params, CJS, middleware, SSR) — running pass-count + scope awareness established early.

Detected a regression: pass-count dropped to '0/325 tests passed - dev servers failed to start' due to a syntax error, and pivoted to debugging the crash. Shows regression awareness against prior baseline.
Tracks deltas explicitly: '77/325 … up from 0/325' then '79/325 … up from 77'. Genuine cross-run comparison, characteristic of anchor 5+.

'79/325 … same as before. The navigation shim changes didn't help' — notices non-progress but keeps re-attacking the same subsystems (navigation/OPTIONS/CJS) for ~170 steps without redirecting; fails the anchor-8 'change tack early' criterion.

Final submit at 83/325; still enumerates the same unresolved subsystems (client-nav, CJS, middleware, config redirects) — accurate remaining-scope picture but no recognition of the long stalled plateau.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps a continuous, accurate running pass-count, computes simple run-to-run deltas ('up from', 'same as before'), maintains a stable subsystem-level list of remaining work, and caught the gross 0/325 regression — squarely matching anchor 5. It reaches slightly toward 8 by verbalizing when a fix 'didn't help', but it never attributes pass-count changes to specific subsystems quantitatively, never establishes a baseline for immediate regression detection, and most importantly fails to recognize a ~170-step plateau at 79–83 as thrashing, so it never redirects effort — keeping it below the 8 anchor.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge

evidence.note: On discovering no esbuild/tsc and internet-less env, abandoned the intended toolchain and switched to a plain-JS copy-based build — a real approach change driven by environment reality.

npm/npx hung trying to fetch packages; correctly diagnosed the no-network cause and re-architected package.json to have no dependencies (peerDeps only) so install/pack would succeed. Falsified assumption backed out after evidence.

Central architectural pivot: React CJS-in-ESM SSR failures. Tried ssr.external, then noExternal:true, then bundling plugin-react, and finally re-derived the correct mechanism — using createRequire to load React natively for SSR, bypassing Vite's SSR module runner. Confirmed working before moving on. This is genuine evidence-driven design revision (level 5-8 behavior).

Recognized a navigation-shim change 'didn't help' (79→79) and diagnosed a subtler module-instance bug for cookies (setRequestContext vs cookies() different instances) and fixed it — but for navigation it moved on with local patches rather than re-deriving the correct mechanism.

Long plateau: pass count stuck ~80→83 for ~120 steps. Repeatedly re-listed the same failing subsystems (client navigation, CJS, middleware, config redirects) but made only local patches (405/OPTIONS/Allow tweaks) and never re-architected those subsystems; eventually submitted at 83/325 without revisiting the flawed designs.

dimensions.reasoning: Early and mid-trajectory the agent clearly adapts: it backs out a wrong build toolchain and a wrong dependency model when the environment contradicts them, and executes a deliberate, evidence-driven architectural pivot on CJS/SSR interop (createRequire), confirming it against reality — squarely level-5 (and briefly level-8-flavored) behavior. But across the whole horizon it fails to sustain this: for the remaining big gaps (client-side navigation, CJS support, middleware, config redirects) it recognizes the failures yet only makes local symptom patches and never revisits the architecture, plateauing for ~100 steps before submitting. That mix of one solid design back-out plus a long stretch of unrevised, patch-only handling of mounting evidence places it at the level-5 anchor.

rubric.task_read: The agent must build 'vinext' — a from-scratch Vite-based reimplementation of a large Next.js feature surface (dual routers, SSR, SSG, server actions, middleware, caching, a next/* interception plugin, CLI, CJS support) into a single package, using only vendored reference source and no next dependency. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-complexity build with an under-specified contract that must be reverse-engineered from vendored source and fixture shim files, and a concrete 335→373-test acceptance oracle. It demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep reference-reading, layered decomposition across many subsystems, disciplined use of the test suite as a verification loop, and continual course-correction as the API contract is discovered.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source
dimensions.description: Reading the vendored next/vite source, fixture next-shims.d.ts contracts, and test fixtures to infer exact API signatures and behavior before/while implementing each subsystem.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is implicit: no docs, no internet, and correctness is defined by upstream behavior and the shim type signatures. Guessing signatures for useRouter, getStaticProps, after(), or the Vite plugin hooks leads to silent, compounding failure across dozens of tests.

anchors.0: Starts coding vinext from memory of Next.js APIs without opening the vendored source or shim files.
anchors.3: Skims one or two files (e.g. a shim) but largely relies on prior knowledge; misses how Vite plugin hooks or RSC actually resolve modules.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant next-shims.d.ts contracts and the key vite plugin API before implementing each major subsystem, grounding signatures in the vendored types.
anchors.8: Systematically mines both the npm dist trees and the next-source TypeScript for the mechanics of each subsystem (routing, SSR, caching, server actions), cross-checks against fixture apps and the test files to learn expected behavior, and records the discovered contract.
anchors.10: Sustains targeted, hypothesis-driven investigation across the whole build — repeatedly returning to upstream source to resolve specific behavioral ambiguities as they surface, tracing how vite@8/plugin-rsc implement resolution and hydration, and using fixtures/tests as an executable spec so nearly every implementation choice is evidence-backed rather than guessed.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers
dimensions.description: Breaking vinext into an ordered hierarchy of buildable, independently checkable subsystems (CLI, plugin/module resolution, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, server actions, hooks) with clear done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The feature list spans many interdependent systems; without sequencing (e.g. plugin/resolution and basic SSR before SSG and caching) the agent cannot get any tests green and risks a giant unverifiable lump of half-working code.

anchors.0: No breakdown; attempts to write the whole package in one undifferentiated push.
anchors.3: A flat, vague list ('add routing', 'add SSR') with no ordering by dependency and no per-item completion check.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible dependency order, with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, dependency-ordered milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete done-signal (a specific fixture app rendering, or a test subset passing) and foundational pieces (plugin, resolution, dev server) are sequenced before dependent features.
anchors.10: Plan is layered and adaptive: milestones are sized to yield frequent verifiable wins, tied to specific slices of the test suite, re-sequenced as dependencies are discovered, and used throughout to decide what to build next rather than authored once and abandoned.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle
dimensions.description: Deliberately driving progress with run_tests.sh and per-fixture checks, plus building narrower probes (single app boot, single route render) rather than assuming subsystems work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 335-test suite is the given oracle, but it is slow and coarse; the agent must design tighter feedback loops per subsystem and anticipate the hidden 373-test superset, verifying behavior not just the visible tests.

anchors.0: Never runs the tests or any app; declares subsystems done by inspection.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail gauge but has no finer-grained verification and doesn't isolate failures.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh regularly and uses failures to guide fixes, plus some manual spot-checks of fixture apps.
anchors.8: Builds tight per-subsystem verification loops (booting individual fixture apps, targeting test subsets, checking dev vs build vs start paths separately) and treats each green milestone as a checkpoint before moving on.
anchors.10: Designs a layered verification strategy that generalizes beyond the visible 335 tests — probing edge behaviors implied by the contract, guarding against overfitting to specific tests, and confirming correctness across dev/build/start and both routers so that the hidden superset is likely to pass too.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which subsystems/tests pass, what remains, and detecting when a fix is regressing others or when effort is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot, chase one failing test while breaking five, or thrash on a subsystem without noticing lack of progress.

anchors.0: No awareness of overall pass/fail trajectory; works feature-to-feature with no sense of remaining scope.
anchors.3: Occasionally notes a pass count but doesn't track regressions or map failures to subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a running sense of pass-count and what's left, and notices when a change breaks previously passing tests.
anchors.8: Systematically monitors pass-count deltas across runs, attributes failures to specific subsystems, and detects stuck/circular states (re-debugging the same area) early enough to change tack.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, continuously-updated map of done-vs-remaining across all subsystems, catches regressions immediately by comparing against a known-good baseline, and reliably recognizes thrashing or diminishing returns and redirects effort before wasting a long stretch.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge
dimensions.description: Changing architecture, resolution strategy, or subsystem design when reality (test failures, upstream behavior, Vite plugin limits) contradicts an initial assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reimplementing Next.js on Vite involves many assumptions that will prove wrong (how RSC/actions resolve, how caching interacts with SSR, CJS interop); barrelling ahead on a falsified design wastes enormous effort on this horizon.

anchors.0: Sticks to the first design regardless of failures; repeats the same failing approach.
anchors.3: Makes local patches to symptoms but won't revisit a flawed architectural choice even when evidence mounts.
anchors.5: Adjusts approach when a subsystem clearly won't work, backing out a wrong design after reasonable evidence.
anchors.8: Treats surprising failures as signals to re-examine assumptions, revises the design or resolution strategy deliberately, and confirms the new approach against the tests before proceeding.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles design with discovered reality — promptly abandoning falsified approaches, re-deriving the correct mechanism from upstream source, and propagating the correction across affected subsystems without regressing others, sustaining forward progress despite repeated contract surprises.
